SQL hooks: SQL hooks (hooks.yaml before_/on_ insert, update, delete) on a command's write tables run inside the command transaction exactly as for an ordinary CRUD write: same reviewed hooks.yaml (the copy the execution digest covers, never a later file; tables match hook keys exactly, like CRUD), same `when:` evaluation and single-pass templating, before-hooks against the pre-write state (a refusal aborts the whole command: no business row, no hook row, no receipt; the attempt is recorded as failed (hook_refused) and the operation stays unconsumed), on-hooks after each write with old_<column> values; a rollback undoes the hook effects. Insert and delete on-hooks also run in the transaction and a failure aborts the command (stricter than ordinary CRUD, which queues those as post-commit jobs). Hook writes are not separately audited, as in CRUD. The command name is available to SQL after-hooks: `command_hook_context`.

What a hook may write: a hook may write revision-enrolled tables (enrolled automatically from hooks.yaml) and `_benmore_notifications`; hook SQL can never reach the operation/approval stores, schema, other pragmas or non-enrolled tables.

Statement shape: hooked statements must write one table with a single `id` primary key and no authored RETURNING, and a table that has hooks for any action refuses ON CONFLICT, OR REPLACE and REPLACE INTO in command SQL (they would skip update/delete hooks), at declaration time and again at run time. A webhook-subscribed table needs the same shape (one table, single id primary key, no RETURNING, no upsert shape).

Hook refusal: a hook refusal or failure returns the distinct code hook_refused (the author's bounded before-hook message is carried for a refusal) and is logged with the operation id prefix and table.

Queued deliveries: delivery work is queued, not run, in the command transaction. An on-hook with a non-SQL action (email, sms, webhook, notify, ws) and every matching active webhook subscription on a written table is enqueued as a durable job with the same payloads and `when:` evaluation as an ordinary CRUD write, so a failed enqueue rolls the whole command back (hook_refused; no business row, no receipt) and nothing is delivered before COMMIT. Only the worker delivers, after commit. Replaying _commit returns the receipt and queues nothing.

Delivery authority: each queued job carries the committing grant id, operation id, owner and write epochs and the command permissions (never a token). Before delivery the worker requires that grant to exist, be unrevoked and unexpired and carry the current owner epoch, the owner approved-writes switch to be on with the same write epoch, and the grant's current actor to still hold the command permissions; otherwise the job fails with error `blocked: ...` (status blocked), is never retried or delivered, and the business mutation is never re-run. The admin job retry (POST /api/_jobs/{id}/retry) refuses a failed effect job with 409, so neither a blocked nor an unknown-outcome effect can be replayed.

Effect status: the status and the receipt report downstream effects as effects: {status, items}. effects.items lists each durable effect the command queued as {id, kind (hook, webhook, flow or transfer), target (table.action), status}, and effects.status is none, pending, delivered, failed, blocked or unknown (any pending item first, then unknown, blocked, failed; delivered only when every item is). The receipt seals effect identity and target, plus a payload digest for transfer effects; status is read from job and transfer-state rows, so it can change after commit while the receipt remains immutable.

Effect outcomes: pending (queued, running, or retrying); delivered when a job completes, or for transfers when durable state proves the push or attach completed (a later verified push reconciliation can prove delivery even if the original job is failed/unknown); failed (hook failures and dropped subscription deliveries); blocked; and unknown (job row gone, a lease that lapsed, or a worker that died mid-run). An interrupted effect job is not requeued: it fails closed as unknown when its outcome cannot be proven, except an event flow declared idempotent, which may be requeued under that flow's policy. A hook effect that fails is not retried (a partial run could send twice).

Delivery evidence: hook and subscription POSTs succeed only on HTTP 2xx; redirects and permanent client errors fail. Ordinary subscription jobs may retry response-confirmed 408, 429 and 5xx; approved-command effects never blindly replay a failed POST. A lost transport response persists an unknown outcome with a fixed non-sensitive error and requires reconciliation; the committed business mutation remains committed.

Refused at commit: a hook that mixes SQL with a delivery action (its SQL would run after commit outside the transaction), non-SQL before-hooks and before-hooks that write, and unsupported write kinds.

CRUD parity: approved commands preserve CRUD validator, computed/encrypted-field, workflow-role-guard and event-flow behavior through the transactional mutation pipeline; event flows are queued atomically with the command, and encrypted readback obeys caller unmask rules. A queued event flow carries the written row's request taint, so its sql_dynamic and enqueue guards refuse command-written columns exactly as for a CRUD write.

Record locks: a command update or delete that would touch a row another user holds a live edit lock on is refused as conflict (retry once the lock lapses), as PATCH refuses it; while such a lock exists the statement needs the hooked shape (one table, single id primary key, no RETURNING, no upsert).
Real-time: after a CONFIRMED commit only (never rollback, replay or unknown), the written tables and hook-written app tables broadcast real-time events.
